controversies.summary: Medieval theologians agreed that faith and reason come from the same God, but disagreed about how far reason reaches. The realist "via antiqua" of Thomists (and Scotists) held that reason can demonstrate God’s existence and grasp real natures; the nominalist "via moderna" of Ockham and Biel limited demonstration and grounded the order of salvation in God’s free covenant. The debate shaped the Reformation, the Catholic revival of Thomism and modern disputes about natural theology.

sides.name: Via antiqua (Thomist realism)
sides.steelman: The God who gave us Scripture also gave us minds. Creation bears the marks of its Maker, so reason can know that God exists and grasp the natural law, even though the Trinity and incarnation exceed it. Faith and reason cannot contradict each other; philosophy rightly used is the handmaid of theology, and grace does not destroy nature but perfects it.
arguments: Romans 1:20: God’s invisible attributes are clearly seen through creation
Unity of truth: God is author of both reason and revelation
Natural law makes public moral reasoning possible
counterArguments: Aristotle’s categories may distort the gospel
Univocity and nominalist logic undermine analogy

sides.name: Via moderna (nominalism) and its Reformation heirs
sides.steelman: God is free and not bound by our philosophical necessities. What he does, he does by his own will and promise. Reason can analyse terms and arguments, but it cannot demonstrate the deep things of God; we know them by revelation. Honesty about reason’s limits honours God’s sovereignty and protects faith from depending on Aristotle.
arguments: God’s absolute power is limited only by contradiction
Many articles of faith are indemonstrable
counterArguments: Covenant of "doing what is in one" sounds semi-Pelagian
Weakens the knowability of natures and morality

sides.name: Enlightenment rationalism
sides.steelman: If reason is God’s gift, it must judge every claim to revelation. Whatever in religion is contrary to reason cannot be from God, and the core of true religion is what every rational person can know: God, virtue and immortality.
arguments: Religious wars show the danger of unverifiable dogma
counterArguments: Reason itself is historically situated and fallen
Butler and Hume showed natural religion is no easier to prove
keyTexts: Kant, Religion within the Bounds of Mere Reason (1793)

timeline.text: Tertullian asks what Athens has to do with Jerusalem.
Anselm’s Proslogion: faith seeking understanding and the ontological argument.
Abelard condemned at Sens after Bernard’s attack on his dialectic.
Aquinas begins the Summa Theologiae.
Paris condemnations stress God’s absolute freedom.
Ockham summoned to Avignon to answer charges about his teaching.
Luther’s Disputation against Scholastic Theology attacks Biel and Aristotle.
Toland’s Christianity not Mysterious opens the Deist controversy.
Vatican I teaches that God can be known with certainty by the natural light of reason (Dei Filius).
Aeterni Patris makes Thomism normative for Catholic schools.
Barth’s "Nein!" to Brunner rejects natural theology.
John Paul II’s encyclical Fides et Ratio describes faith and reason as two wings by which the spirit rises to truth.

resolution.text: Catholic teaching (Vatican I, Fides et Ratio) affirms reason’s capacity to know God while giving Aquinas special honour. Protestant traditions range from Reformed and Lutheran scholastic use of natural theology to Barthian rejection of it; Orthodox theology stresses apophatic and experiential knowledge. The question remains open across traditions.

consequences: Shaped the theological background of the Reformation.
Defined Catholic seminary education from 1879 to the 1960s.
Continues in debates over natural theology, intelligent design and public reason.

controversies.question: Does theology begin from human religious experience and history, or from God’s self-revelation alone?
controversies.title: Liberal versus neo-orthodox (dialectical) theology
controversies.summary: Liberal Protestantism, from Schleiermacher to Harnack, rebuilt theology on religious experience, historical study and ethics. After 1914 Karl Barth and the dialectical theologians rejected this as making God a projection of human culture, insisting that God is known only in his self-revelation in Jesus Christ. Their public exchange in 1923 and the Church struggle in Nazi Germany made the dispute a defining one for 20th-century Protestantism.

sides.name: Liberal Protestantism
sides.steelman: Faith must be honest. Modern people cannot simply repeat ancient creeds or treat the Bible as an oracle; historical study shows how doctrines grew. Yet the essence of Christianity shines through: the God-consciousness of Jesus, the fatherhood of God, the infinite worth of the soul and the Kingdom of love. Theology must speak to educated culture and be accountable to reason and history, or it becomes arbitrary.
arguments: Religious experience as universal human reality
Ethical fruit of the Kingdom of God
counterArguments: Reduces God to human feeling or culture
keyTexts: Schleiermacher, On Religion (1799); The Christian Faith (1821-22)

sides.name: Dialectical theology (neo-orthodoxy)
sides.steelman: God is not the highest point of human religion but the wholly other who speaks. When the leading liberal theologians signed the 1914 manifesto supporting the Kaiser’s war, it became clear that a theology built on culture would bless culture. Theology’s only ground is the Word of God, Jesus Christ, attested in Scripture and proclaimed in the Church; historical study serves but cannot judge it.
arguments: Infinite qualitative difference between God and humanity (Kierkegaard)
Revelation is God’s free act, not a human possession
Barmen 1934 showed its power to resist idolatry
counterArguments: Risk of fideism and isolation from other disciplines
Ambiguity about Scripture’s inspiration and history
keyTexts: Barth, The Epistle to the Romans (1919, 1922)

timeline.text: Schleiermacher’s Speeches on Religion.
Ritschl completes Justification and Reconciliation.
Harnack lectures on the essence of Christianity in Berlin.
Harnack and other theologians sign the "Manifesto of the Ninety-Three" supporting German war aims; Barth is appalled.
Barth’s Epistle to the Romans "falls like a bomb on the playground of the theologians".
Barth and Harnack exchange open letters in Die Christliche Welt.
Barmen Declaration of the Confessing Church.
Bultmann’s demythologising lecture opens a new phase.

resolution.text: Dialectical theology dominated mid-century Protestant academies, but liberal, existentialist, process and revisionist theologies continued, and evangelicals criticised both. Many later theologians (postliberals, Moltmann, Pannenberg) sought paths beyond the opposition.

consequences: Shaped the Confessing Church and the ecumenical movement.
Divided American Protestantism between liberal, neo-orthodox and evangelical options.
Influenced postliberal theology.
